title: Surgical Treatment of Adjacent Segment Stenosis
summary:
Lumbar spine surgery is among the most frequently performed surgical procedures. In Germany alone, more than 314,000 such operations were performed in 2021. In addition to minimally invasive procedures, the number of lumbar fusion surgeries has increased substantially. However, lumbar fusion surgery is associated with greater blood loss, longer hospital stays, and higher morbidity compared with minimally invasive procedures. Furthermore, lumbar fusion significantly alters the biomechanical properties of the spine. The implanted instrumentation may increase mechanical stress on adjacent spinal segments. In addition, loss of paraspinal musculature and iatrogenic scar formation may impair spinal stability. This may lead to the feared late complication known as adjacent segment disease (ASD). ASD includes degenerative disc disease, hypertrophy of the facet joints, hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum, and ultimately nerve compression due to spinal canal stenosis at the adjacent segment (“adjacent segment stenosis”, ASS). As a consequence, patients may experience clinical deterioration and worsening pain months or years after the initial fusion surgery. The reported incidence of ASD after lumbar fusion ranges from 5% to 27%. Conservative treatment of neurogenic claudication and back pain caused by spinal canal stenosis is often unsuccessful, making additional surgery necessary in the majority of cases.

The current surgical standard for the treatment of ASS consists of decompression of the spinal canal combined with extension of the spinal fusion to the affected adjacent segment. However, this procedure may further impair the paraspinal musculature and again alter the biomechanical loading of the spine. A vicious cycle may develop, resulting in repeated instrumentation surgeries, prolonged hospitalizations, and increasing pain-related disability. Alternatively, a minimally invasive microsurgical decompression procedure can be performed without extending the fusion while preserving biomechanically important structures such as intervertebral discs, ligaments, and facet joints.

In patients with primary degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis without prior surgery, several studies have demonstrated that minimally invasive decompression alone is superior to decompression combined with fusion. These studies showed shorter operative times, shorter hospital stays, and fewer complications. However, the situation following prior lumbar fusion is viewed differently because surgical decision-making is based on the assumption that the adjacent segment may be unstable and therefore require additional fusion.

The aim of this study is to investigate whether decompression alone is non-inferior to decompression with fusion extension in patients with adjacent segment stenosis. A total of 338 patients in Germany and Austria will be included. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two treatment groups (control group: decompression with fusion; intervention group: decompression alone).

Follow-up examinations will be performed 6, 12, and 24 months after surgery. The primary endpoint of the study is physical disability at 24 months, assessed using the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI).
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Age ≥ 18 years
- Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) at screening 30–80% (ODI ≥ 30% and ODI ≤ 80%)
- Symptomatic adjacent segment stenosis following degenerative lumbar fusion surgery that has not responded to at least 6 weeks of qualified conservative treatment
- MRI evidence of spinal canal stenosis at the adjacent segment following lumbar fusion surgery
- Capacity to provide informed consent and ability to complete the questionnaires
- Written informed consent after comprehensive patient information and counseling
Exclusion criteria:
- Adjacent segment kyphosis or scoliosis (>10°)
- Screw loosening / pseudarthrosis
- Known current pregnancy or breastfeeding
- Acute traumatic injury or fracture of the spine
- Active inflammatory or neoplastic disease of the spine
- Contraindication to spinal surgery
- Inability to provide complete and comprehensible informed consent due to language barriers, even with the assistance of an interpreter (as the questionnaires used in the study have been validated in the German language only)
- Symptoms related to spinal canal stenosis are not the patient’s leading clinical symptom
- Neuroforaminal stenosis grade ≥ 2 according to Lee et al. (Lee S, Lee JW, Yeom JS, et al. A practical MRI grading system for lumbar foraminal stenosis. AJR Am J Roentgenol. Apr 2010;194(4):1095–1098. doi:10.2214/AJR.09.2772)
- Dynamic spondylolisthesis ≥ 3 mm on flexion-extension radiographs
- Persons institutionalized by judicial or governmental order
